How to read notes on the staff

The height of a note on the five lines of the staff tells you its pitch. Once you know where one note is, you can count up and down to the others, one step for each line and space. This page shows the notes of the treble and bass clef, with a name under every note.

Lines and spaces

The staff has five lines and four spaces between them. A note sits either on a line (the line goes through it) or in a space. Going up from a line to the next space, or from a space to the next line, is one step in the alphabet: C, D, E, F, G, A, B, and then C again.

The clef at the start of the staff says which note is where. Without it, the lines have no names.

Treble clef (G clef)

The treble clef curls around the second line from the bottom: that line is G (the G above middle C), which is why it is also called the G clef. It is used for the right hand on the piano, for most singers, and for violin, flute, trumpet, and recorder.

  • Lines, from the bottom: E G B D F, “Every Good Boy Does Fine”.
  • Spaces, from the bottom: F A C E, which spells “FACE”.

Bass clef (F clef)

The two dots of the bass clef sit on either side of the fourth line from the bottom: that line is F (the F below middle C), so it is also called the F clef. It is used for the left hand on the piano, and for cello, bassoon, trombone, and low voices.

  • Lines, from the bottom: G B D F A, “Good Boys Do Fine Always”.
  • Spaces, from the bottom: A C E G, “All Cows Eat Grass”.
WhereNotes, from the bottom
Treble clef, linesE – G – B – D – F
Treble clef, spacesF – A – C – E
Bass clef, linesG – B – D – F – A
Bass clef, spacesA – C – E – G

Middle C and ledger lines

Notes above or below the staff get short extra lines, called ledger lines. Middle C (the C near the middle of the piano, C4) is written on one ledger line just below the treble staff, and on one ledger line just above the bass staff. In a piano score the two staves meet at middle C, so it is a good note to find first.

Reading faster

  • Use landmarks. Learn a few notes by heart (middle C, the G of the treble clef, the F of the bass clef) and count steps from the nearest one.
  • Read the shape. Notes that move line → space → line go up or down one step at a time; a jump from line to line skips one note.
  • Check the key signature. The sharps and flats at the start of each line change some notes everywhere in the piece. See sharps, flats, and key signatures.

Let the app write the names

Note Namer writes the name under every note of a photographed score, with the sharps and flats of the key signature already included. Use it to check your own reading: name a line yourself, then compare. The names can be letters (C D E), Do Re Mi, ドレミ, or 도레미 (see the note name chart), and the page can be printed. See the guide.
